property_summary: Only the owner can successfully call sendTo (calls by non-owners revert).
When InvMutTest calls c.sendTo(receiver, amount) the call must revert (reverted == true) for this contract's caller.
When this test contract calls c.sendTo(receiver, amount), the call must revert (reverted == true).
When InvMutTest calls c.sendTo(receiver, amount) the call must revert (reverted == true).

Invariant: only the contract owner can successfully invoke sendTo(address,uint256) (i.e., calls by non-owners do not transfer Ether and therefore do not change contract balance); the mutant removing the require allows any caller to transfer funds and thus violates this owner-only rule for some inputs.

For every input, only the deploying owner can cause C.sendTo(...) to succeed and transfer contract balance; the mutant removing the owner check allows non-owners to invoke sendTo(...) and thus can transfer funds for some inputs, violating the owner-only transfer rule.

For every caller and amount, when sendTo is invoked the call only succeeds (transfers contract balance) if msg.sender is the owner; removing the require allows some non-owner callers to succeed and thus changes address(c).balance for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller and amount, calling sendTo(receiver, amount) either always succeeds only when invoked by the stored owner (so non-owners cannot make the contract transfer funds), whereas the mutant removing the require allows a non-owner adversary to succeed and change address(c).balance for some fuzzed amount/caller; the test checks that a non-owner call cannot transfer the contract's balance (reference holds for all inputs, mutant broken for some).

For every (caller,receiver,amount) where the contract has a positive balance >= amount, only the owner can cause the contract to successfully send Ether (i.e., sendTo only succeeds when msg.sender == owner); removing the require allows a non-owner attacker contract to drain funds for some fuzzed inputs, so the mutant violates this owner-only-send rule.
Only the contract owner can initiate a successful sendTo call (i.e., sendTo succeeds only when msg.sender == owner).

sendTo reverts iff the provided receiver is not the contract owner (i.e., calls succeed for any caller as long as receiver equals owner in the mutant, but in the original success does not depend on receiver), so the test asserts that in the original implementation sendTo never reverts solely because receiver != owner.
If the call from this test to c.sendTo reverts then receiver must not equal address(this).
If the test's call to c.sendTo reverts then the receiver address must not equal this test contract's address.
If the call to c.sendTo(receiver, amount) reverts then receiver must not equal address(this).

Reference: only the contract owner can CALL sendTo successfully (calls by non-owner revert); mutant: requires receiver==owner instead, so non-owner callers may succeed when sending to owner — violating the caller-authorization rule.

For every caller and receiver, only the contract owner can successfully call sendTo (i.e., calls from non-owner always revert); the mutant instead allows non-owners to succeed when the receiver is the owner, breaking this caller-authorisation property.

For any caller and any receiver+amount, only calls originating from the contract owner succeed (non-owners' calls always revert); the mutant instead allows non-owners to succeed when the receiver equals owner, breaking this caller-authorization rule.

For every caller and receiver+amount, calling sendTo succeeds if and only if msg.sender == owner (so only the owner can make sendTo succeed); the mutant instead allows non-owners to succeed when receiver == owner, violating that caller-authorization rule.

For every caller and receiver+amount, if sendTo succeeds (does not revert) then the caller must be the contract owner; the mutant allows non-owners to succeed when the receiver equals owner, breaking this rule.
Only the owner can successfully send out ether from contract C (calls to sendTo by owner succeed, non-owner calls revert).
Calls to c.sendTo by the contract owner never revert, while calls by non-owners always revert (i.e., reverted == (msg.sender != owner)).
If the caller is the contract owner then c.sendTo does not revert; if the caller is not the owner then c.sendTo reverts.
The call to c.sendTo must not revert (i.e., reverted == false) for the inputs supplied to run.
The call to c.sendTo with the provided inputs must not revert (reverted == false).
For every caller and amount, only the owner is allowed to successfully invoke sendTo (calls from non-owners must revert); the mutant inverts this check and allows non-owners while blocking the owner.

For any caller who is the owner and any amount, calling sendTo must forward the specified amount out of the contract (reflected in address(c).balance change); the mutant early-returns when amount == 0 causing no transfer for that case.

For any receiver and amount, if the contract has at least `amount` wei balance and the caller is the owner, then after calling sendTo(receiver, amount) the contract's balance decreases by exactly `amount` (the buggy mutant returns early when amount==0 and thus can leave the balance unchanged for amount==0), so the property will fail for amount == 0 on the mutant.

For any caller who is the owner and any receiver and amount, calling sendTo transfers the specified amount out of the contract so address(c).balance decreases by exactly amount; the mutant early-returns when amount == 0 and thus can leave the balance unchanged for amount == 0, violating the rule for that input.

If the owner sends a nonzero amount from C to a receiver, the contract's balance decreases by exactly that amount; the mutant early-returns only for amount==0 and so can violate this rule for zero amounts, so we restrict the domain to amount > 0.

For every caller who is owner and any receiver and amount, calling sendTo transfers exactly that amount out of the contract (so address(c).balance decreases by amount); the mutant early-returns when amount == 0 causing no transfer for amount==0 and thus violating the rule for that input.

For any caller who is owner and any receiver/amount, after sendTo is called the contract's balance decreases by exactly amount (i.e., funds are forwarded to a party other than the contract itself), but the mutant that always sends to owner changes observed post-call behavior (address(c).balance change will still be amount but receiver vs owner recipient differs) — we detect the mutation by checking that when the receiver is not the owner, the contract's balance still decreases by amount and the call succeeds (reference) whereas mutant still succeeds but the receiver's balance does not increase; specifically we assert that if the caller is owner and receiver != owner then the receiver's balance increases by amount (reference) which the mutant breaks for some inputs.
